tools.name: Python 3 (standard library)
tools.reason: The starter is Python; the data are 126 rows. csv, statistics-style arithmetic, http.server, unittest and json cover everything, so the project has zero third-party dependencies and runs anywhere Python runs.

tools.name: csv module
tools.reason: Reads the CSV row by row, which lets every malformed row be counted and excluded individually; a dataframe loader would coerce or drop bad rows silently.

tools.name: unittest
tools.reason: Already used by the starter (`python -m unittest discover`); needs no installation. Existing tests are kept unchanged.

tools.name: http.server + vanilla JS/SVG
tools.reason: A small read-only JSON API and a hand-built SVG chart give a real interactive demo without Node, bundlers or CDNs, and the same service code feeds CLI, API and tests.

tools.name: Playwright + Microsoft Edge
tools.reason: Used to drive the real UI, cross-check displayed numbers against the API and capture desktop/mobile screenshots. It is not a dependency of the weather app.

tools.name: Git
tools.reason: Local clone of upstream main as baseline, development branch and commit; used for the Draft PR flow.

tools.name: pandas / numpy
tools.reason: Unnecessary for 42 daily values per city; they would hide per-row validation and add a heavy dependency. Availability on this machine is listed in Environment.

tools.name: scikit-learn / statsmodels / deep learning
tools.reason: A transparent baseline is requested. With 29 training points per city a fitted model could not be validated and would be harder to explain; the repeating pattern is captured by a one-line seasonal rule.

tools.name: Live weather API
tools.reason: Optional in the requirements; the task is to forecast from the supplied synthetic dataset, and real data would contradict the synthetic-data labelling.

method.name: Seasonal naive with drift (selected per city from five transparent candidates)
method.why: The series repeat a 12-day up-ramp. The autocorrelation of the training data alone peaks at lag 12 (0.57 for Tokyo). The candidates were compared by rolling-origin backtest inside the training set only; seasonal naive with drift had the lowest error, so it was selected without looking at held-out data.
method.how: Prediction for day t+h = observed value one 12-day cycle earlier + average cycle-to-cycle change measured so far. Example: Tokyo day 1 (2026-09-12) = 17.5 (2026-08-31) + 0.21 = 17.7 °C.
method.limitations: The cycle is an artefact of the synthetic generator. Real weather does not repeat on a fixed schedule, so this method has no real-world forecasting claim. There is no uncertainty interval.
method.why_not_ml: 42 daily points per city (29 for training) is too little to fit and validate a learned model, and the supplied pattern is captured exactly by a seasonal rule. A model would be less transparent and its extra complexity could not be justified by the evaluation.

limitations: All observations are synthetic. Nothing produced here is a real weather forecast.
The ~0.06 °C held-out MAE reflects the regular 12-day pattern built into the synthetic data, not real forecasting skill.
Small data: 42 daily observations per city (29 train / 13 held out); the cycle length is estimated from 29 training days.
Held-out MAE is the same for horizons 1–3 because the method copies the value one cycle earlier.
Only temperature is forecast; humidity and rain are unused and no uncertainty interval is given.
The repository is an imported ZIP snapshot; remote publication depends on GitHub credentials (see GitHub tab).
